questions.stem: Where in a cell does aerobic respiration mainly take place?

options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
The nucleus stores genetic instructions; it is not where glucose is broken down.
Ribosomes assemble proteins rather than releasing energy.
The membrane manages what enters and leaves, not energy release.

questions.stem: Which substances leave aerobic respiration as waste products?

options.explanation: These are the inputs consumed, not the outputs released.
Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Lactic acid belongs to the oxygen-free pathway in animal cells.
That pair comes from yeast respiring without oxygen.

questions.stem: Why does the aerobic route release more energy from one glucose molecule?

options.text: Because mitochondria multiply during the process
options.explanation: Organelle numbers are not what raises the yield.

options.text: Because carbon dioxide stores the spare energy
options.explanation: Carbon dioxide is a low-energy waste, not a store.

options.text: The glucose is broken down completely, so far fewer usable bonds remain unharvested
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Because oxygen itself is a fuel
options.explanation: Oxygen enables the oxidation; it is not an energy source on its own.

questions.stem: Which statement about aerobic respiration is true for plant roots at midnight?

options.text: It stops because photosynthesis has stopped
options.explanation: Respiration runs independently of photosynthesis in the dark.

options.text: It switches to using sunlight directly
options.explanation: Cells cannot power reactions with raw sunlight.
Every living plant cell, roots included, respires.

options.text: Root cells keep running it because every living cell needs ATP around the clock
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: What does aerobic respiration hand to the cell for it to spend?

options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Glucose is the fuel consumed, not the currency released.
Oxygen is consumed as the oxidant.
Proteins are a nutrient class, not the energy currency here.

questions.stem: State the word equation for the aerobic breakdown of glucose.
questions.modelAnswer: Glucose plus oxygen gives carbon dioxide and water, with energy transferred to ATP.

questions.stem: Name the organelle where aerobic respiration happens and the gas it consumes.
questions.modelAnswer: It happens in the mitochondria and consumes oxygen.

questions.stem: Explain why aerobic respiration transfers more energy than the oxygen-free route.
questions.modelAnswer: Oxygen allows the complete oxidation of glucose, so almost all the bond energy is harvested into ATP, whereas partial breakdown leaves energy locked in the products.

questions.stem: A jogger's leg muscles carry on aerobic respiration throughout a steady run. Describe what the cells take in and give out.
questions.modelAnswer: They take in oxygen and glucose, break the glucose down completely inside mitochondria, and release carbon dioxide and water while transferring energy into ATP for contraction.

questions.stem: How many oxygen molecules react with one glucose molecule in the balanced aerobic equation?

options.explanation: Two is far too few to oxidise one glucose fully.
Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Four oxygens would leave the atom count unbalanced.
Twelve doubles what the equation requires.

questions.stem: What is the correct symbol equation for aerobic respiration?

options.explanation: Oxygen is missing; the aerobic route cannot run without it.
The reactants and products are swapped around.
Correct — this matches the account taught above.
That runs the opposite way and describes photosynthesis.

questions.stem: Which substances sit on the right-hand side of the aerobic symbol equation?

options.explanation: Those are the reactants on the left.
Ethanol belongs to fermentation, not this route.
Lactic acid is the animal oxygen-free product.
Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: A student answers a 'balanced symbol equation' question using words only. What follows?

options.text: No credit, because the command word demands chemical formulas
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Full credit if the words are in the right order
options.explanation: The mark scheme requires the symbols themselves.
Schemes do not award partial marks for the wrong form.

options.text: Credit once the spelling is correct
options.explanation: Spelling does not substitute for the required formulas.

questions.stem: Why must the symbol equation be balanced?

options.text: So that energy can be shown
options.explanation: Energy is not part of the balancing rule.

options.text: Atoms are conserved, so every atom entering must appear among the products
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: To make the equation look longer
options.explanation: Length has nothing to do with validity.

options.text: Because oxygen always comes in sixes
options.explanation: The sixes follow from conservation, not habit.

questions.stem: Write the balanced symbol equation for aerobic respiration.
State how many carbon dioxide molecules form from one glucose molecule.
questions.modelAnswer: Six carbon dioxide molecules form for every glucose respired aerobically.

questions.stem: Explain why answering with words alone is risky when the question asks for a symbol equation.
questions.modelAnswer: Because the command word requires chemical formulas, and only the formulas carry the atom counts that balancing proves.

questions.stem: A classmate writes C6H12O6 + O2 -> CO2 + H2O. Correct the line and justify your edit.
questions.modelAnswer: Insert the sixes: C6H12O6 + 6O2 -> 6CO2 + 6H2O, since one glucose needs six oxygens and yields six of each product, keeping atoms conserved.

questions.stem: What builds up in hard-working muscle cells when oxygen runs short?

options.explanation: Carbon dioxide dominates the aerobic route, not this one.
Glycogen is the storage carbohydrate, not the waste here.
Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Yeast makes ethanol; animal cells do not.

questions.stem: How does the energy yield of the oxygen-free route compare, per glucose?

options.text: Larger, since glucose is handled faster
options.explanation: Speed does not raise the yield; completeness does.
The incomplete split leaves energy behind.

options.text: Zero, because no oxygen is used
options.explanation: A little ATP is still transferred.

options.text: Much smaller, because the breakdown stops partway
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

questions.stem: Why can sustained lactic acid accumulation harm performance?

options.text: It lowers muscle pH, and acidic conditions can denature enzymes
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: It raises muscle pH, blocking nerves
options.explanation: The shift is toward acidity, not alkalinity.
Membranes do not melt; enzymes lose their shape.
The acid is later broken down using oxygen, not bound by it.

questions.stem: Which word equation describes the oxygen-free pathway in animal cells?

options.explanation: Those are the aerobic products.
Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
That is the plant and yeast version.
Oxygen is absent from this route by definition.

questions.stem: During a sprint, why do muscle cells still run some aerobic respiration?

options.text: The oxygen-free route replaces it completely
options.explanation: Both operate; the second tops up the shortfall.

options.text: Muscles stop needing energy at high intensity
options.explanation: Demand rises, which is exactly why both engage.

options.text: Oxygen supply persists but cannot fully match demand, so both routes run side by side
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: The aerobic route shuts down entirely in sprints
options.explanation: It continues, contributing most of the steady ATP.

questions.stem: State the fate of lactic acid once exercise ends.
questions.modelAnswer: Oxygen breaks the lactic acid down into carbon dioxide and water.

questions.stem: Name the compound whose partial breakdown defines the animal oxygen-free route.
questions.modelAnswer: Glucose is only partially broken down, leaving lactic acid.

questions.stem: Explain why the oxygen-free route transfers only a little ATP per glucose.
questions.modelAnswer: Because glucose is not fully oxidised; energy remains stored in the lactic acid molecules that leave the pathway.

questions.stem: A swimmer's shoulders ache near the end of a race. Use both respiration routes to explain the ache.
questions.modelAnswer: Sustained effort outpaces oxygen delivery, so the muscles add the oxygen-free route and produce lactic acid; its build-up lowers the tissue pH, and that acidic environment is sensed as the ache.

questions.stem: Which products form when yeast respire without oxygen?

options.explanation: Animal cells make lactic acid; yeast does not.
Oxygen is a reactant in the aerobic route, never a product here.
Neither belongs to any respiration pathway.
Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

questions.stem: What is fermentation?

options.text: The oxygen-free breakdown of glucose by yeast
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Any breakdown of glucose in leaves
options.explanation: The term is tied to yeast and similar fungi.
Bread uses fermentation, but fermentation itself needs no oxygen.

options.text: The conversion of starch into glucose
options.explanation: That is digestion, not fermentation.

questions.stem: In bread-making, which fermentation product lifts the dough?

options.explanation: ATP powers the yeast cells, not the expansion of the dough.
Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Ethanol evaporates during baking; it does not raise the dough.
Water is not the raising agent.

questions.stem: Which row of a respiration comparison table is stated correctly?

options.explanation: Lactic acid versus ethanol and carbon dioxide differ.
The oxygen-free yield is smaller.

options.text: Oxygen used: aerobic yes, oxygen-free no
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Aerobic is the complete one.

questions.stem: Why does the oxygen-free route in plants leave ethanol behind?

options.text: Ethanol is a store the plant reuses for photosynthesis
options.explanation: It is a waste of this route, not a fuel store.
The two simply coexist as products.

options.text: Plants lack mitochondria for full breakdown
options.explanation: Plant cells have mitochondria; the route differs because oxygen is absent.

options.text: The glucose is only partly broken down, so carbon and energy stay in the ethanol
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

questions.stem: State the word equation for the oxygen-free route in yeast.
questions.modelAnswer: Glucose gives ethanol and carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: Name one industry example that relies on fermentation.
questions.modelAnswer: Bread-making relies on the carbon dioxide released by yeast fermentation.

questions.stem: Explain why the two routes share one comparison table yet produce different wastes.
questions.modelAnswer: Because the presence or absence of oxygen decides how far glucose is oxidised, and each stopping point defines a different waste product.

questions.stem: A baker notices dough rising faster in a warm kitchen. Explain the biology behind the observation.
questions.modelAnswer: Warmth speeds yeast fermentation, so more carbon dioxide is released per minute, inflating the dough quicker.
